draft.title: Divergent, convergent and transform boundaries
card: Divergent
Plates move apart. Where this happens on the sea floor, a ridge forms. Where it happens on land, a rift valley can form.
Convergent
Plates push towards each other. Mountains can form where plates crumple upwards, and a deep ocean trench can form where one plate sinks under another.
Transform
Plates slide past each other sideways. Crust is not pulled apart or pushed together, and the boundary is marked by a line of broken rock.
A boundary is named by how the plates move relative to each other: apart, together or side by side.
draft.remember: The name of a boundary tells you how the plates move: apart, together or past each other.

a.q: Two plates on the sea floor are moving away from each other and a ridge is forming. What type of boundary is this?
a.why: Plates moving apart form a divergent boundary, and a ridge is one landform that results. A convergent boundary is wrong because there the plates push together, not apart.
a.clue: Think about the direction the plates are moving.

b.q: Two plates meet. One is sinking under the other, and a deep trench lies along the line where they meet. How are the plates moving, and what is the boundary?
b.why: A trench forms where one plate sinks under another, so the plates are pushing together. This is a convergent boundary. A divergent boundary is tempting because the sea floor can look deep and low there too, but plates at a divergent boundary move apart and do not sink.
b.clue: A plate sinking under another is being pushed towards it.

problems.detail: The why says a divergent boundary is tempting because the sea floor 'can look deep and low there too'. The card teaches that a ridge forms where plates move apart on the sea floor, and mid-ocean ridges are raised. This contradicts the card and could mislead students.

check.summary: The card and both questions are accurate, and each has one clear right answer. The why for question b wrongly suggests the sea floor looks deep and low at divergent boundaries, which contradicts the card's point that a ridge forms there.
